name: Urdu

script.overview:
Urdu is written **right to left** in an extended Perso-Arabic alphabet of about 38 letters, plus the aspiration marker **ھ** (do-chashmī he) and the nasal **ں** (nūn ġunna). Printed and handwritten Urdu normally uses the **Nastaliq** style, in which words slope down from upper right to lower left and letters stack diagonally; newspapers, phones and computers use Nastaliq too, though you will also see the upright *Naskh* style.

Urdu is a joined (cursive) script. Most letters connect to the letter before **and** after them, and so they have up to four shapes: isolated, initial, medial and final. But **nine letters never join to the following letter**: ا د ڈ ذ ر ڑ ز ژ و (and ے, which only occurs at the end of a word). After one of these, the next letter starts a fresh 'chunk' even in the middle of a word — so a word like اردو is written as four separate pieces: ا · ر · د · و (all four are non-connectors).

Many letters share the same basic shape and differ only in **dots** (nuqte): ب پ ت ٹ ث are all the same 'boat' shape with one, three or two dots or a small ط. Learn the shapes in families and then the dots.

Urdu is an *abjad*-like script: **long vowels are written** with ا (ā), و (ū, o, au) and ی/ے (ī, e, ai), but **short vowels a, i, u are usually left out**. They can be marked with small diacritics (zabar, zer, pesh) — beginners' books and the Qur'an use them, but ordinary text does not. Several sounds are written with more than one letter (four letters for z, three for s, two each for t and h) because Urdu keeps the original spelling of Arabic and Persian loanwords.

Digits ۰–۹ are written **left to right** even inside right-to-left text, just like in English.

groups.title: Alif and the 'be' family
groups.note: Alif is the first letter and a non-connector. ب پ ت ٹ ث share one 'boat' shape and differ only in dots. In the middle of a word the boat shrinks to a small tooth with its dots.

letters.sound: alif. At the start of a word it is a 'carrier' for a short vowel (a, i or u); elsewhere it is long ā as in 'father'. Non-connector: never joins to the letter after it (final form ـا).
letters.strokes: One straight stroke from top to bottom, slightly slanted.

letters.sound: be. Like English b. Joins both ways: initial بـ and medial ـبـ are just a small tooth with one dot below.
letters.strokes: A shallow boat drawn right to left with a little upturned tail on the right; one dot underneath.

letters.sound: pe. Like English p but with no puff of breath (compare پھ ph). Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The boat shape with three dots below in a triangle.

letters.sound: te. A dental t: the tongue tip touches the back of the upper teeth, softer than English t, no puff of breath. Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The boat shape with two dots above, side by side.

letters.sound: ṭe. A retroflex t: curl the tongue tip back and tap the roof of the mouth. Sounds 'harder' and more English-like than ت. Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The boat shape with a small ط (a tiny loop with a stalk) above instead of dots.

letters.sound: se. Pronounced exactly like س (s). Found only in Arabic loanwords. Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The boat shape with three dots above in a triangle.

groups.title: The 'jīm' family
groups.note: Four letters with the same hooked shape: dot below (ج), three dots below (چ), no dot (ح), dot above (خ). Initial and medial forms lose the big lower bowl.

letters.sound: jīm. Like English j in 'jam'. Joins both ways; initial form جـ.
letters.strokes: A short horizontal stroke to the left, then a sharp turn into a big open bowl curving down and right; one dot inside the bowl.

letters.sound: che. Like ch in 'church' but without a strong puff of breath. Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The jīm shape with three dots inside the bowl.

letters.sound: baṛī he ('big h'). In Urdu pronounced just like ہ — an ordinary h. Arabic loanwords only. Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The jīm shape with no dots.

letters.sound: xe. A rasping sound at the back of the mouth, like ch in Scottish 'loch' or German 'Bach'. Not the same as کھ kh! Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The jīm shape with one dot above the top stroke.

groups.title: The 'dāl' family (non-connectors)
groups.note: A small angled shape that sits on the line. These letters join to the letter before them but NEVER to the letter after them.

letters.sound: dāl. A dental d, tongue against the upper teeth. Non-connector.
letters.strokes: A short stroke down-left, then a horizontal stroke to the left — like a small angled '<' leaning back.

letters.sound: ḍāl. A retroflex d: tongue tip curled back to the roof of the mouth. Closer to English d than د is. Non-connector.
letters.strokes: The dāl shape with a small ط on top.

letters.sound: zāl. Pronounced z in Urdu (in Arabic it was 'th' as in 'this'). Arabic loanwords. Non-connector.
letters.strokes: The dāl shape with one dot above.

groups.title: The 're' family (non-connectors)
groups.note: A curved stroke that dips below the line. Like dāl, these never join to the following letter.

letters.sound: re. A light tap of the tongue tip behind the teeth, like the tt in American 'butter' or a Spanish r. Always pronounced, never silent. Non-connector.
letters.strokes: A short curved stroke starting on the line and sweeping down and to the left, like a comma.

letters.sound: ṛe. A retroflex flap: curl the tongue back, then flick it forward so it strikes the roof of the mouth once. Never starts a word. Non-connector.
letters.strokes: The re shape with a small ط on top.

letters.sound: ze. Like English z. The most common of Urdu's four z letters. Non-connector.
letters.strokes: The re shape with one dot above.

letters.sound: zhe. Like the s in 'measure'. Very rare — a few Persian and French/English loanwords. Non-connector.
letters.strokes: The re shape with three dots above.

groups.title: The 'sīn', 'su’ād' and 'to’e' families
groups.note: س ش have three little teeth; ص ض have a flat loop; ط ظ have the loop plus an upright stalk. Several of these are pronounced identically — they mostly mark Arabic loanwords.

letters.sound: sīn. Like English s. Joins both ways; in the middle of a word it is just three small teeth (ـسـ).
letters.strokes: Three small teeth from right to left, then a deep bowl like the end of ن.

letters.sound: shīn. Like English sh. Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The sīn shape with three dots above the teeth.

letters.sound: su’ād. Pronounced s, just like س. Arabic loanwords. Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: A flat oval loop drawn clockwise, a tiny tooth, then a deep bowl.

letters.sound: zu’ād. Pronounced z in Urdu. Arabic loanwords. Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The su’ād shape with one dot above the loop.

letters.sound: to’e. Pronounced like ت (dental t). Arabic loanwords. Joins both ways; the shape does not change much.
letters.strokes: A flat oval loop, then an upright stalk added on the left from top to bottom.

letters.sound: zo’e. Pronounced z. Arabic loanwords. Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The to’e shape with one dot to the right of the stalk.

groups.title: The 'ʿain', 'fe' and 'qāf' families
groups.note: ع غ have a small open mouth at the top; ف ق have a round head (one dot for ف, two for ق) and differ in their tails.

letters.sound: ʿain. In Arabic a throat sound; in everyday Urdu it is usually silent or just a slight catch, and it often lengthens or colours a neighbouring vowel (بعد baʿd sounds like 'bād'). Joins both ways; medial form ـعـ is a small closed triangle.
letters.strokes: A small open 'c' shape at the top, then a big bowl curving below like jīm.

letters.sound: ġain. A gargled g made at the back of the throat, like a French or German r. Not the same as گھ gh! Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The ʿain shape with a dot above.

letters.sound: fe. Like English f (some speakers say a light ph). Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: A small round loop with one dot above, then a flat tail to the left.

letters.sound: qāf. A k made much further back, where the tongue meets the uvula — a 'deeper', hollow k. Many speakers soften it to k in casual speech. Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: A small round loop with two dots above, then a deep round bowl below the line.

groups.title: The 'kāf', 'lām', 'mīm', 'nūn' letters
groups.note: ک گ are tall with a slanted top stroke (گ has two). ل is a tall hook, م a small round head with a tail, ن a bowl with a dot. ں is ن without the dot and only at the end of words.

letters.sound: kāf. Like English k but without a puff of breath. Joins both ways. Note: Urdu ک is different from the Arabic ك — it never has the small squiggle inside the bowl.
letters.strokes: A long diagonal stroke from upper left down to the right, then a flat base back to the left.

letters.sound: gāf. Like g in 'go' (always hard). Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: The kāf shape with a second short diagonal line above the first.

letters.sound: lām. A clear l with the tongue on the teeth ridge, as in 'leaf' (never the dark l of 'full'). Joins both ways.
letters.strokes: A tall vertical stroke down, curving into a round bowl at the bottom.

letters.sound: mīm. Like English m. Joins both ways; medial form is a small closed loop.
letters.strokes: A small round loop, then a short tail straight down.

letters.sound: nūn. Like English n (dental). Joins both ways; initial and medial forms are a small tooth with a dot above.
letters.strokes: A round bowl like a smile, with one dot inside above it.

letters.sound: nūn ġunna. Not a consonant: it makes the preceding vowel nasal (air through the nose), like French 'non'. Only at the end of a word; in the middle of a word ordinary ن (often written without its dot by hand) does the job.
letters.strokes: The nūn bowl without the dot.

groups.title: Vā’o, the two he's, hamza and the two ye's
groups.note: و is a non-connector and does double duty as consonant v and long vowels ū/o/au. ی and ے do double duty as consonant y and the vowels ī/e/ai. ہ (round he) and ھ (two-eyed he) look similar but have different jobs.

letters.sound: vā’o. As a consonant, a soft v/w (between English v and w). As a vowel: ū ('moon'), o ('go') or au ('law'). Non-connector.
letters.strokes: A small round head like a closed loop, then a tail sweeping down to the left (like a big comma).

letters.sound: choṭī he ('little h') or gol he ('round h'). An ordinary breathy h. At the end of a word after a consonant it usually stands for a short -a (کمرہ kamra 'room'). Joins both ways; its shapes change a lot: initial ہـ, medial ـہـ, final ـہ.
letters.strokes: Isolated: a small loop with a tail, like a teardrop on its side.

letters.sound: do-chashmī he ('two-eyed h'). Not used alone: it is written after a consonant to make it aspirated (breathy) — ب + ھ = بھ bh, ک + ھ = کھ kh. Always connects to the preceding letter.
letters.strokes: A round shape with two small 'eyes' (loops) inside, drawn as one continuous loop that crosses itself.

letters.sound: hamza. Marks a break between two vowels (آئیے ā’iye) rather than a real consonant; in Urdu it is mostly heard as a glide. Sits on a 'chair' ئ in the middle of words, alone ء at the end. Also used above ہ/ے for the izāfat ('of') link.
letters.strokes: A small backwards '2'-like squiggle, written above the line.

letters.sound: choṭī ye ('little ye'). Consonant y, or the long vowel ī ('see'). In the middle of a word it also writes e and ai. Joins both ways; initial/medial form is a tooth with two dots below.
letters.strokes: Isolated: a curl to the left that swings back right in a deep 'S'-like tail below the line.

letters.sound: baṛī ye ('big ye'). Only at the end of a word, for e ('café') or ai ('bat'). It joins to the letter before it but nothing can follow it. Very common: ہے hai, کے ke, سے se.
letters.strokes: A small hook, then a long straight stroke sweeping back to the right below the line.

groups.title: Aspirated consonants (with do-chashmī he ھ)
groups.note: Urdu has a whole series of breathy consonants written as a letter + ھ. They are single sounds, not 'consonant + h'. Many writers also use ہ for the rarer nasal/liquid ones (تمہارا for تمھارا). Aspiration changes meaning: کان kān 'ear' vs کھان khān 'mine'.

letters.sound: A breathy b — say b with a murmur of breath, as in 'club house' run together.
letters.strokes: Write ب (initial form) and attach ھ.

letters.sound: p with a strong puff of air, like p in English 'pin'. Never f.
letters.strokes: پ + ھ.

letters.sound: Dental t with a puff of air. Never English 'th'.
letters.strokes: ت + ھ.

letters.sound: Retroflex ṭ with a puff of air.
letters.strokes: ٹ + ھ.

letters.sound: A breathy j.
letters.strokes: ج + ھ.

letters.sound: ch with a strong puff of air.
letters.strokes: چ + ھ.

letters.sound: A breathy dental d.
letters.strokes: د + ھ (د doesn't join forward, but ھ still attaches to it in print as a ligature).

letters.sound: A breathy retroflex ḍ.
letters.strokes: ڈ + ھ.

letters.sound: A breathy retroflex flap. Never starts a word.
letters.strokes: ڑ + ھ.

letters.sound: k with a strong puff of air, like k in 'kit'. Not the same as خ x.
letters.strokes: ک + ھ.

letters.sound: A breathy g, like 'doghouse' run together. Not the same as غ ġ.
letters.strokes: گ + ھ.

letters.sound: A breathy m. Usually written مہ.
letters.strokes: م + ھ.

letters.sound: A breathy n. Usually written نہ.
letters.strokes: ن + ھ.

groups.title: Writing vowels
groups.note: Long vowels are written with letters; short vowels usually aren't written at all. At the start of a word every vowel needs alif (or ع) as a carrier.

letters.sound: alif madd: long ā at the start of a word ('father'). In the middle or end of a word ā is plain ا.
letters.strokes: Alif with a wavy madd line on top.

letters.sound: Short a, like the u in 'but'. Written with zabar (usually omitted).
letters.strokes: Alif with a small diagonal stroke above.

letters.sound: Short i, as in 'sit'. Written with zer (usually omitted).
letters.strokes: Alif with a small diagonal stroke below.

letters.sound: Short u, as in 'put'. Written with pesh (usually omitted).
letters.strokes: Alif with a tiny و-shaped curl above.

letters.sound: Long ī, as in 'see'. Written with ی (یـ in the middle of a word).
letters.strokes: Alif + initial ye.

letters.sound: Long e, as in 'café' (a pure vowel, no glide). Written ے at the end of a word, یـ in the middle.
letters.strokes: Alif + baṛī ye.

letters.sound: ai, like the a in 'bat' (in some areas closer to 'bet'). Same letters as e; zabar can mark it.
letters.strokes: Alif with zabar + ye.

letters.sound: Long o, as in 'go' (pure, no glide).
letters.strokes: Alif + vā’o.

letters.sound: Long ū, as in 'moon'. Same letter as o; pesh can mark it.
letters.strokes: Alif with pesh + vā’o.

letters.sound: au, like the aw in 'law'. Same letter as o and ū; zabar can mark it.
letters.strokes: Alif with zabar + vā’o.

groups.title: Diacritics (e‘rāb) and special marks
groups.note: Small marks above and below letters. Everyday Urdu leaves most of them out; dictionaries, children's books and poetry use them to show exact pronunciation.

letters.sound: zabar: a short slanting stroke above the letter = short a.
letters.strokes: One short stroke above, slanting down to the left.

letters.sound: zer: the same stroke below the letter = short i. Also used as the izāfat 'of' link in Persian phrases (وزیرِ اعظم vazīr-e aʿzam 'prime minister').
letters.strokes: One short stroke below the letter.

letters.sound: pesh: a tiny vā’o above the letter = short u.
letters.strokes: A tiny curl like a miniature و above the letter.

letters.sound: jazm: a small circle or arc above a letter = no vowel follows it (it closes the syllable).
letters.strokes: A small round or half-moon mark above the letter.

letters.sound: tashdīd: a small 'w' shape above = the consonant is doubled (held longer). Changes meaning: پتا patā 'address' vs پتّا pattā 'leaf'.
letters.strokes: A small 'w' (three tiny teeth) above the letter.

letters.sound: tanvīn (do-zabar): two zabars on a final alif = -an. Only in Arabic adverbs.
letters.strokes: Two parallel zabar strokes above the final alif.

letters.sound: khaṛā zabar ('standing zabar'): a small vertical alif above a letter = long ā, in a few Arabic words.
letters.strokes: A tiny upright stroke above the letter.

letters.sound: hamza-e izāfat: a small hamza on a final ہ (or ے/ئے) links two nouns Persian-style, meaning 'of'.
letters.strokes: Write ہ, then a small ء above it.

letters.sound: madd: the wavy line over alif (آ) that makes a long ā at the start of a word or after a vowel.
letters.strokes: A short wavy horizontal line above alif.

groups.title: Common letter combinations and ligatures
groups.note: In Nastaliq, letters join and stack into characteristic shapes. These everyday combinations are worth recognising at a glance — many are the commonest little words in the language.

letters.sound: lām-alif: lām + alif fuse into a special 'V'-like shape.
letters.strokes: Two strokes rising from a shared base, crossing like a V.

letters.sound: kāf + alif: 'of' (masculine). The kāf's top stroke leans over the alif.
kāf + ye: 'of' (feminine); the ye sweeps back under the kāf.
kāf + baṛī ye: 'of' (masc. plural / oblique).
he + baṛī ye: 'is'. Probably the most frequent word you'll read.
'are': he + ye + nūn ġunna.
Spelled the same for 'I' (maiṃ) and 'in' (meṃ) — context tells you which.
'no, not': nūn + he + ye + nūn ġunna, stacked diagonally.
The ergative marker (Unit 16): nūn + baṛī ye.
'from, with, than': sīn + baṛī ye.
'also, too': be + do-chashmī he + ye.
'was': te + do-chashmī he + alif.
'this, he/she/it (near)'. Spelled ye + he but pronounced ye (formally yah).
'that, he/she/it (far)'. Spelled vā’o + he, pronounced vo (formally voh).
A special ligature with tashdīd and khaṛā zabar, often in phrases like ان شاء اللہ.

groups.title: Urdu digits ۰–۹
groups.note: Urdu uses Eastern Arabic-Indic digits in their Urdu/Persian forms (note ۴ ۵ ۶ ۷ look different from Arabic ٤ ٥ ٦ ٧). Numbers are written left to right. Western digits 0–9 are also very common in Pakistan, especially for prices and phone numbers.

letters.sound: zero: a small dot (or tiny circle).
letters.strokes: A dot.

letters.sound: one: a vertical stroke.
letters.strokes: One vertical stroke top to bottom.

letters.sound: two: a stroke with one hook at the top right.
letters.strokes: A hook at top, then down.

letters.sound: three: a stroke with two hooks at the top.
letters.strokes: Two little teeth at top, then down.

letters.sound: four: Urdu form with a loop and a tail (different from Arabic ٤).
letters.strokes: A small loop, then a curved tail down.

letters.sound: five: Urdu form is a pointed teardrop (Arabic ٥ is a circle).
letters.strokes: An upside-down heart/teardrop shape.

letters.sound: six: Urdu form with a tail curving to the left at the bottom.
letters.strokes: A small hook at top, stroke down, tail to the left.

letters.sound: seven: Urdu form looks like a 'V' with a small hook on the left arm.
letters.strokes: A V shape, the left arm hooked.

letters.sound: eight: an upside-down V (Λ).
letters.strokes: Two strokes meeting at the top.

letters.sound: nine: a small loop at the top with a vertical stem.
letters.strokes: A small loop, then a stroke straight down.

where: National language of Pakistan; official in several Indian states (Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, J&K and others); spoken by large diaspora communities in the UK, Gulf, USA and Canada
tagline: The language of ghazals, Bollywood lyrics and everyday Pakistan — and once you speak it, you can understand spoken Hindi too.
intro:
**Urdu** (اردو) is an Indo-Aryan language that grew up in north India between the 13th and 18th centuries, mixing the everyday speech of the Delhi region with a large vocabulary from **Persian** and **Arabic** (and some Turkish). Today it is the national language and lingua franca of Pakistan and the mother tongue of tens of millions of people in India.

In everyday conversation Urdu and **Hindi** are essentially the same language — same grammar, same basic words — so learning to speak one means you can talk with speakers of the other. They differ in script (Urdu uses a Perso-Arabic script, Hindi uses Devanagari) and in their formal and literary vocabulary: Urdu draws on Persian and Arabic where Hindi draws on Sanskrit.

Urdu is written **right to left** in the flowing, slanted *Nastaliq* style. Short vowels are normally not written, so you learn words as whole shapes. Urdu is also famously polite: there are three words for 'you' (**آپ** āp, **تم** tum, **تو** tū), and choosing the right one matters.

This course teaches the **standard modern spoken Urdu** heard in Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad, Hyderabad and Lucknow. Every word comes with romanization, but we strongly encourage you to learn the script alongside it — it is much easier than it looks.
romanizationNote: Romanization shows how words are actually pronounced. A bar marks long vowels (ā ī ū); plain a i u are short (a = the 'u' of 'but'). e and o are always long, like 'café' and 'go'; ai is like 'bat' (or 'bet') and au like 'law'. A dot under t d r (ṭ ḍ ṛ) means a retroflex sound with the tongue curled back; plain t d are dental (tongue on the teeth). An h after a consonant (kh, gh, ph, th, bh…) means aspiration — a puff of breath — so th is never English 'th' and ph is never 'f'. The Persian/Arabic sounds are q (ق, deep in the throat), x (خ, as in Scottish 'loch'), ġ (غ, a gargled g), ʿ (ع) and ’ (ء), which today are usually just vowel breaks. ṃ after a vowel means the vowel is nasalised (ہاں hāṃ). A silent final ہ after a consonant is written -a (کمرہ kamra), and -ah in a few words where the h is traditionally kept (بارہ bārah, سالگرہ sālgirah). Note that the script often doesn't show short vowels, so the romanization is your guide to them.

pronunciation.title: Short vowels are usually not written
pronunciation.body:
Ordinary Urdu writing shows consonants and long vowels (ā ī ū e o ai au) but leaves out the short vowels a, i, u. So کم could in principle be kam, kim or kum — but in practice it is *kam* 'less', and you simply learn each word's pronunciation. This is exactly how English speakers learn that 'read' can be reed or red.

Two consequences for learners: first, **always learn the romanization along with the script** when you meet a new word. Second, don't 'read in' vowels that aren't there: سمجھ is samajh, not sa-ma-ja-ha; کتاب is kitāb, with i after k and a long ā written by alif.

The most common short vowel is a (like 'u' in 'but'). Also note the very common pattern where a written ہ at the end of a word stands for a short final -a: کمرہ kamra 'room', بچہ bachcha 'child'.
tips: When a dictionary or children's book shows zabar/zer/pesh, use them to check your guesses.
Final ہ after a consonant is usually -a: کمرہ kamra, پردہ parda.
Learn words as whole shapes — after a few weeks you'll recognise کتاب or شکریہ instantly.
Short a sounds like the 'u' in 'cup', never like the 'a' in 'cat'.

pairs.note: Same letters د ل; only the unwritten vowel differs.
Both written کل in ordinary text.
Both written سر in ordinary text.

pronunciation.title: Short and long vowels
pronunciation.body:
Urdu contrasts short a, i, u with long ā, ī, ū, and the difference changes meaning. The long vowels are not just longer — they also have a different quality: short a is the 'u' of 'cup', long ā is the 'a' of 'father'; short i is 'sit', long ī is 'seat'; short u is 'put', long ū is 'boot'.

The vowels e and o are always long and pure — no English glide at the end. Say *e* like 'café' (not 'cay-ee') and *o* like Scottish 'go' (not 'goh-oo'). The vowels ai and au are single sounds too: ai is like 'bat' (Lahore and Karachi) and au like 'law'.

The good news: long vowels are always written (ا و ی ے), so the script tells you when a vowel is long.
tips: Exaggerate the length of ā at first: kāaam.
Keep e and o steady — don't let them slide into 'ay-ee' or 'oh-oo'.
ai in ہے hai sounds like English 'heh' or 'hæ', not 'high'.
au in اور aur sounds like 'or' in British English without the r-colour, not 'hour'.

pronunciation.title: Aspiration: k vs kh, p vs ph, t vs th…
pronunciation.body:
Urdu distinguishes plain consonants from aspirated ones — consonants followed by a strong puff of breath. Aspirated letters are written with **ھ** (do-chashmī he): کھ kh, پھ ph, تھ th, ٹھ ṭh, چھ chh. There are also breathy-voiced ones: بھ bh, دھ dh, ڈھ ḍh, جھ jh, گھ gh, ڑھ ṛh.

English actually has both kinds of k, p and t — the p in 'pin' is aspirated, the p in 'spin' is not — but English speakers don't notice the difference. In Urdu it changes meaning: کان kān 'ear' but کھان khān 'mine (quarry)'. So you need to learn to produce **plain** k, p, t, ch with *no* puff (as after s in English) and aspirated ones with a *big* puff.

Remember: th is never English 'th', and ph is never 'f'. And kh (کھ) is not x (خ).
tips: Hold a tissue in front of your mouth: it should stay still for پ p and flutter for پھ ph.
For plain p/t/k, imagine an s before them: 'spa', 'star', 'sky'.
For bh, dh, gh, say the consonant with a sigh, like 'abhor' or 'doghouse'.
Don't confuse کھ kh with خ x: kh is a k with a puff; x is a scrape in the throat.

pronunciation.title: Retroflex ٹ ڈ vs dental ت د
pronunciation.body:
Urdu has two kinds of t and d. The **dental** ones, ت t and د d, are made with the tongue tip pressed against the back of the upper front teeth — softer than English t/d. The **retroflex** ones, ٹ ṭ and ڈ ḍ (marked with a small ط on top), are made with the tongue tip curled back to touch the roof of the mouth behind the gum ridge.

English t and d fall in between, which is why Urdu speakers hear English t/d as retroflex: 'TV' becomes ٹی وی, 'doctor' becomes ڈاکٹر. So if you use your normal English t/d you will sound fine for ٹ ڈ but wrong for ت د. Concentrate on making ت د truly dental — almost like a lisped t.

Retroflex sounds appear in many everyday native words: ٹھیک ṭhīk 'OK', ڈر ḍar 'fear', چھوٹا chhoṭā 'small'.
tips: For ت د, put the tongue tip firmly against your teeth, as if about to say 'th' — then make a t/d.
For ٹ ڈ, curl the tongue back and strike the roof of the mouth with its underside.
English loanwords use the retroflex series: ٹکٹ ṭikaṭ 'ticket', ڈاکٹر ḍākṭar.
Practise in pairs, slowly, then fast.

pronunciation.title: The flaps ڑ ṛ and ڑھ ṛh, and the tapped ر r
pronunciation.body:
Urdu ر r is a single quick tap of the tongue tip behind the teeth, like the tt in American 'better' or a Spanish r. It is always pronounced, even at the end of a word (گھر ghar has a real r) — never silent as in British English.

ڑ ṛ is a different sound: curl the tongue tip back (as for ٹ ڈ) and then flick it forward so that the underside slaps the roof of the mouth on the way out. It never starts a word; it appears between vowels or at the end: بڑا baṛā 'big', گاڑی gāṛī 'car', پہاڑ pahāṛ 'mountain'. ڑھ ṛh is the same with a breathy release: پڑھنا paṛhnā 'to read'.

The contrast between ر, ڑ and ڈ matters: ڈ is a full stop (the tongue holds), ڑ is a flick.
tips: Say 'butter' the American way — that middle sound is close to ر.
For ڑ, start with the tongue curled back as if for 'rr' and flick it down and forward.
Never pronounce English 'r' (with rounded lips and bunched tongue) in Urdu.
Keep final r: گھر ghar, سر sar, اور aur.

pairs.note: Also a vowel difference — but the flick vs tap is the key.

pronunciation.title: Nasal vowels with ں
pronunciation.body:
A vowel can be pronounced with air flowing through the nose as well as the mouth — a nasal vowel, like French 'bon' or the 'uh-uh' sound of English 'no'. In Urdu this is written with **ں** (nūn ġunna, nūn without a dot) at the end of a word, and with an ordinary ن (often undotted in handwriting) in the middle.

Nasalization is grammatically important: it marks plural verbs and many grammatical endings. ہے hai 'is' vs ہیں haiṃ 'are'; کہا kahā 'said' vs کہاں kahāṃ 'where'; میں maiṃ 'I'. There is no n consonant here — don't say 'hain' with a full n; just let the vowel go through the nose.

Before a stop consonant, a nasal vowel often sounds like a short nasal consonant: پانچ pāṃch 'five', اونٹ ūnṭ 'camel'.
tips: Pinch your nose: for a nasal vowel the sound should change; for a plain vowel it shouldn't.
Don't close your mouth or touch the tongue to the roof at the end of ہیں — it's a vowel, not 'n'.
ں is always at the end of a word; ن with a dot is a real n.
Listen for nasal endings on verbs: ہوں hūṃ, ہیں haiṃ, جائیں jā’eṃ.

pronunciation.title: ق q vs ک k
pronunciation.body:
ق q is made further back than k: the back of the tongue touches the uvula (the little dangling thing at the back of the mouth) instead of the soft palate. It sounds deeper and more 'hollow', and it tends to pull neighbouring vowels back: قلم qalam sounds a bit like 'qulum'.

In careful and educated speech, and in Pakistan generally, q is kept distinct. In very casual speech and in many Indian varieties it merges with k (so you will hear 'kalam'). Learn to make q — it signals good Urdu — but don't worry if you hear k.
tips: Say 'k' and slide the contact point as far back as you can, almost to a gargle — but with a full stop.
Practise 'kaw-kaw-qaw-qaw', feeling the tongue move back.
Most words with ق are Arabic: وقت vaqt, قیمت qīmat, حقیقت haqīqat.

pronunciation.title: خ x, غ ġ vs کھ kh, گھ gh
pronunciation.body:
These four are a classic beginners' trap because the romanization of many older books writes خ as 'kh' and غ as 'gh'. In this course **kh and gh always mean the aspirated stops** کھ گھ, and **x and ġ mean the fricatives** خ غ.

خ x is a continuous scraping sound at the back of the mouth, like Scottish 'loch' or German 'Bach' — your tongue never fully closes. غ ġ is the voiced version — like a French r or gargling. By contrast, کھ kh is a k (full closure!) with a puff of air, and گھ gh is a g with breathy release.

خ and غ come from Persian and Arabic and are very common in everyday words: خوش xush 'happy', خبر xabar 'news', غلط ġalat 'wrong', باغ bāġ 'garden'.
tips: For خ, say 'k' but don't let the tongue touch — let the air hiss through.
For غ, do the same with your voice on, like gargling gently.
For کھ and گھ, there is a clear stop, then a release with breath.
Casual speakers sometimes say خ as kh and غ as g; aim for x and ġ.

pronunciation.title: ع ʿain and ء hamza in practice
pronunciation.body:
In Arabic, ع is a strong throat consonant. In everyday Urdu it is **usually not pronounced as a consonant at all**. Instead it affects the vowels around it: at the start of a word it is simply a vowel carrier (عام ʿām sounds exactly like آم ām 'mango'); after a short a it typically makes the vowel long and open (بعد baʿd → 'bād', شعر shiʿr → 'sher', معلوم maʿlūm → 'mālūm'). Careful speakers, news readers and religious contexts may add a slight catch in the throat.

Hamza ء marks the boundary between two vowels — جائے jā’e, آئیے ā’iye, گائے gā’e — where the voice glides from one vowel to the next. It is not a hard glottal stop in normal speech.

In this course's romanization, ʿ and ’ show you where these letters are, so you can spell the words; in speaking, follow the notes and your ear.
tips: Don't produce an Arabic-style throat sound for ع in casual Urdu — it sounds affected.
aʿ before a consonant usually sounds like a long ā or open 'e': بعد 'bād', شعر 'sher'.
Hamza between vowels = a smooth glide: جائیں 'jā-eṃ'.
Write ع correctly even though you don't hear it — Urdu speakers notice spelling mistakes.

pairs.note: In everyday speech both sound like 'sher'.

pronunciation.title: One sound, several letters: the z's, s's, t's and h's
pronunciation.body:
Because Urdu preserves the Arabic spelling of loanwords, several letters are pronounced the same:

**z** — ز ذ ض ظ (ze, zāl, zu’ād, zo’e). ز is the native and Persian one and by far the most common.
**s** — س ث ص (sīn, se, su’ād). س is the most common.
**t** — ت ط (te, to’e).
**h** — ہ ح (choṭī he, baṛī he).

For speaking this is good news: there are fewer sounds than letters. For writing you just have to learn which letter each word uses — the romanization (z, s, t, h) won't tell you. A useful hint: words with ث ذ ص ض ط ظ ح ع are almost always Arabic in origin.
tips: Learn the spelling with the word: نظر nazar 'sight' has ظ; ضرور zarūr has ض; ذرا zarā has ذ.
Pairs of homophones are distinguished only in writing — like 'right/write' in English.
ژ zh is a separate, rare sound (as in 'measure').

pronunciation.title: Same spelling, different vowels: e/ai and o/ū/au
pronunciation.body:
The letters ی/ے and و each write several vowels. ی in the middle of a word can be ī, e or ai; و can be ū, o or au (or the consonant v). Without diacritics, the spelling doesn't tell you which — some words are even spelled identically: پیر is both pīr 'Monday; saint' and pair 'foot'; بیل is bel 'creeper' and bail 'ox'; سو is so 'sleep!' and sau 'hundred'.

In practice context makes the meaning clear. For pronunciation, remember the qualities: e as in 'café', ai as in 'bat'; o as in 'go' (pure), au as in 'law'.
tips: ai and au are single vowels in standard Urdu, not diphthongs like English 'eye' and 'ow'.
When in doubt, follow the romanization.
Diacritics distinguish them: پَیر pair vs پِیر pīr; سَو sau vs سو so.

pronunciation.title: Double consonants (tashdīd)
pronunciation.body:
A doubled consonant is held for longer before it is released — like the 'k k' in 'bookcase' or the 'n n' in 'unnamed'. In Urdu doubling is common and can change meaning: پتا patā 'address' vs پتّا pattā 'leaf'.

The script marks doubling with tashdīd (ّ), but like the short vowels it is usually left out, so you learn it with the word. Many very common words have it: اچھا achchhā, بچہ bachcha, سچ ہے sach hai vs سچّا sachchā 'true', پکا pakkā 'firm, ripe'.
tips: Pause briefly on the consonant: ach-chhā, pak-kā.
Don't double where there is no doubling — that changes the word too.
Words borrowed from Arabic often have tashdīd: محبت mohabbat, اول avval.

pronunciation.title: Rhythm and question intonation
pronunciation.body:
Urdu stress is light and fairly even — no syllable is shouted and no vowel is swallowed the way English reduces 'banana' to 'b'nana'. Heavy syllables (with a long vowel or ending in a consonant) get slightly more weight: kitāb, ghar, ach-chhā.

Yes/no questions are often identical to statements except for a **rising intonation** at the end: آپ ٹھیک ہیں۔ āp ṭhīk haiṃ (statement) vs آپ ٹھیک ہیں؟ āp ṭhīk haiṃ? (question). You can also start with کیا kyā, which turns the sentence into a yes/no question — it does not mean 'what' here. Question words (کون، کیا، کہاں…) usually sit right before the verb, and the voice rises on the question word.

The little word نا nā at the end of a sentence asks for agreement, like 'right?' or 'isn't it?'.
tips: Don't reduce unstressed vowels to 'uh'.
For yes/no questions, rise at the end — or add کیا at the start.
Add نا at the end to sound friendly and natural: ٹھیک ہے نا؟
Urdu ends statements with ۔ (a dash-like full stop), not a dot.
